text: You get an array nums. You can travel from index i to index j if the gcd of their values is greater than one. Return true if every pair of indices is connected, directly or through other indices.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — this is really a connectivity question. Two numbers can reach each other in one hop when they share a prime factor, because that is exactly when their gcd is above one. Is that the right reading?

One edge to pin down — the value one. The number one has no prime factor, so its gcd with anything is one. So if one shows up and there is more than one element, it can never reach anyone, and the answer is false. And if the array has a single element, there is no pair to connect, so that is true. Good?
Good catches. Constraints: up to ten to the fifth numbers, each up to ten to the fifth.

Let me run through the example. Take four, three, twelve, eight. Four and twelve share two. Three and twelve share three. Eight shares two with four and twelve. So everything hangs together through twelve — that is true. But three, nine, five: three and nine share three, but five is a lone prime, so it is false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to build the graph directly — compare every pair, add an edge when the gcd is above one, then check connectivity. But that is n squared pairs, and with ten to the fifth numbers that is about five billion gcd calls. Way too slow. This problem reminds me of union-find, but with a twist on the nodes. Instead of making the numbers the nodes, I make the prime factors the nodes. Each number ties all of its own prime factors into one group. Two numbers that share a prime then land in the same group for free. At the end, everything is connected exactly when all the primes that appear sit in a single component.

Here's the plan. Prime factors are the union-find nodes. One: sieve the smallest prime factor of every value up to the max. Two: for each number, union all of its prime factors. Three: check that every number's smallest prime shares one root. One thing worth flagging — the sieve gate. When I mark multiples of a prime i, I only write spf of j if it still equals j, meaning nobody has touched it yet. This is the part people get wrong. Primes come in increasing order, so first writer wins gives the smallest prime factor. Gating on equals i is never true, and the sieve would do nothing. There's a trade-off here. Trial division skips the sieve and is fine for a few values, but with many numbers the shared sieve is faster. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The union-find keeps negative sizes in parent, with path compression and union by size. The main function handles a single element and an all-ones array up front, builds the sieve with that gate, then for each number takes its smallest prime as the anchor and unions every prime factor into it, stripping each prime out as it goes. A one anywhere returns false. One thing worth flagging — the final check reads spf of v, not v. I only ever call Union on primes, so a composite like twelve was never a node. Find of twelve would just return twelve and look disconnected. Reading spf of v asks about a prime that really lives inside v's component.

Let's dry-run the code with four, three, twelve, eight. I expect true. The row that matters is twelve. Before it, the primes two and three are two separate islands, so three is stranded. Twelve carries both, so Union of three and two fuses the islands into one, with three as the root. Then the check: the anchor is spf of four, which is two, and every number's smallest prime finds that same root, so true. Let's also test corner cases. A single one is true — no pair to connect. Six and one: the loop hits the one and returns false. Three, nine, five: primes three and five never meet, two components, false.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is big O of A log log A plus n log A, where A is the max value. The sieve is the log log part; each number splits into at most log A primes, and union-find is near constant per call. The space complexity is big O of A, for the two arrays. In the worst case A is about ten to the fifth, so both fit easily. Oh, one more thing — if the values could reach ten to the ninth, the arrays would not fit. I would switch to trial division by primes up to the square root of A, and key the union-find by a hash map instead of an array.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed a quadratic graph into a union-find over prime nodes, so the size collapses. You explained why the sieve gate is spf of j equals j — first writer wins gives the smallest prime factor — and why equals i would silently break it. And you flagged that the final check must read spf of v, since composites were never union nodes. Good work.
